paragraphs.heading: What carbon-14 is
paragraphs.text: Carbon-14, also called radiocarbon or ¹⁴C, is a radioactive isotope of carbon. Its nucleus holds 6 protons and 8 neutrons. Franz Kurie suggested in 1934 that it existed. Martin Kamen and Sam Ruben discovered it in Berkeley on February 27, 1940, working at the University of California Radiation Laboratory.

paragraphs.heading: Where it comes from
paragraphs.text: Most carbon-14 on Earth forms when cosmic rays act on nitrogen in the atmosphere. Production is highest at altitudes of 9 to 15 kilometres and at high geomagnetic latitudes. Lightning makes some too, but globally the amount is negligible next to what cosmic rays produce. Above-ground nuclear tests by several countries between 1955 and 1980 sharply raised the amount in the atmosphere, and then in living things.

paragraphs.heading: How it decays
paragraphs.text: In carbon-14, one neutron turns into a proton while giving off an electron and an electron antineutrino. The atom becomes nitrogen-14, which is stable. The half-life of carbon-14 is 5700 years, give or take 30. The electrons it sends out have fairly low energy, so they travel at most an estimated 22 cm through air, and only 0.27 mm into body tissue.

paragraphs.heading: A clock for the dead
paragraphs.text: Plants take carbon from the air during photosynthesis, so a plant or animal that dies holds roughly the same carbon-14 level as the atmosphere at that time. After that the level falls exponentially, so the date of death can be estimated. Radiocarbon dating uses this to find the age of carbon-bearing material up to about 50,000 years old. Willard Libby and his colleagues developed it in 1949 at the University of Chicago, and Libby won the 1960 Nobel Prize in chemistry for the work. A common use is dating organic remains from archaeological sites.

paragraphs.heading: Checking against tree rings
paragraphs.text: The starting level of carbon-14 for the calculation can be estimated, or taken from records of known age. Tree rings give year-by-year data back to 10,000 years ago, and cave deposits reach back to about 45,000 years before present. Comparing a sample directly with these records gives its age more accurately than a calculation alone.

paragraphs.heading: Measuring tiny amounts
paragraphs.text: Small amounts of carbon-14 are hard to pick up with typical Geiger–Müller detectors. Liquid scintillation counting is the preferred method, though accelerator mass spectrometry has lately become the method of choice. It counts every carbon-14 atom in a sample, not only the few that decay while it is being measured. That lets it work on much smaller samples, even single plant seeds, and it gives results faster.

paragraphs.heading: Tracing and timing
paragraphs.text: The isotopes of carbon hardly differ in their chemistry, so researchers can swap carbon-14 in for nonradioactive carbon and follow it through chemical and biological reactions, a method called carbon labeling. Radiocarbon can also show that carbon stored in peatland soils is being released because of land clearance or climate change. And the spike from the bomb tests made bomb-pulse dating possible, which can work out a person's birth year from the carbon-14 in tooth enamel or in the lens of the eye.
